deep_why: The core insight is combining user-item interaction signals across many different datasets into a single unified space where similarity is meaningful. The mathematical foundation rests on the principle that if you represent interactions as images or visual features, you can measure closeness using the same distance function everywhere—this works because distance in shared visual space is consistent and transitive. Since users and items follow similar behavioral patterns across domains, their visual representations will cluster predictably, allowing new users or items to find relevant matches even without seeing similar cases before. This unified representation lets them scale with more data while handling cold-start and cross-domain problems that plague separate models.

The core being modeled is how multiple expert perspectives on geopolitical events can produce better forecasts than a single viewpoint. The principle underlying this is that diverse expert opinions, when combined carefully, reduce systematic blindspots that any single view would have—each expert captures different aspects of complex causation. This works because geopolitical events depend on many intertwined factors (diplomatic, historical, cultural, economic), and different specialists understand different causal chains. By having multiple experts independently reason and then reconcile their views, errors from one expert's incomplete understanding are corrected by another's stronger insight in that domain. The ensemble outcome more accurately captures the true complexity of what will happen.

The core task is splitting long documents into meaningful chunks that preserve the information someone would need to answer their questions. The soundness rests on the principle that question-aware segmentation respects information dependencies—if a query will ask about some topic, all related context needed to answer it must stay together in one chunk. When domain documents are dense and cross-referenced, naive chunking at fixed positions breaks these dependencies, leaving chunks incomplete. By treating chunking as two parts (splitting at logical topic boundaries, then filling in missing context) guided by question examples, the method ensures chunks are self-contained units. This integrity lets downstream question-answering systems retrieve and use information without having to stitch fragments across multiple chunks.

The core problem is that compressed neural models lose the ability to learn new tasks over time, a drift called plasticity loss. The mathematical reason this happens is that after learning many tasks, the model's remaining internal capacity becomes too rigid—weight changes that help new learning conflict with preserving old knowledge. The method works by temporarily expanding capacity when a new task arrives, giving the model room to make changes without disrupting the old learned behaviors. After learning the new task, pruning removes the temporary expansion, recompressing the model while using a strategy that prioritizes connections most useful for future adaptation. This cycle preserves both compactness and adaptability by treating them as dynamically adjustable rather than permanently fixed.

The core being estimated is how public opinion during crises changes when emotional reactions and deeper beliefs interact. The principle grounding this is that human opinion has two layers working together: immediate feelings (fear, anger) that shift quickly, and underlying convictions (values, ideology) that change slowly. These two interact—emotions can temporarily override convictions, but if convictions are strong enough they eventually pull feelings back toward consistent positions. By modeling both layers and their interaction explicitly, the system can explain why opinions first swing emotionally then partially recover. This dual modeling matches real social dynamics better than single-layer approaches, letting predictions follow actual opinion trajectories through crises.

The core being studied is how short-video consumption follows functional patterns similar to substance addiction despite being behavioral rather than chemical. The principle is that addictive behavior, whether to drugs or media, follows the same economic trade-off curve—as someone consumes more, the satisfaction per unit drops but the drive to consume grows, creating escalation. This happens because the brain's reward system habituates to stimulation in predictable mathematical ways regardless of the source. By combining this economic addiction model with actual user behavior data from the platform, the simulator can learn personalized addiction curves for each user. This lets them test whether algorithmic changes that promote diversity actually reduce engagement escalation across different user types.

The core task is finding location mentions in crisis documents accurately and fairly across all regions. The mathematical principle is that bias in extraction is a property of training data—if training examples skew toward certain regions, the system learns location patterns that over-fit to well-represented places and under-fit to rare ones. Using larger models with few-shot reasoning and context-aware disambiguation works because they can balance between strong general knowledge (learned from diverse training) and specific context clues in each document. By explicitly measuring fairness (performance difference between overrepresented and underrepresented regions), the method exposes and corrects for this learned bias. This produces a system that retrieves locations equally well whether a place is documented often or rarely.

The core being detected is functional differences between identical code when compiled to Web Assembly versus native binaries. The principle underlying this is that different compilation targets expose subtle differences in how numbers are computed, how memory is accessed, and how floating-point rounding works—these differences are inherent to the platforms. By running the same code with the same inputs on both platforms and comparing outputs, any inconsistency reveals a discrepancy rooted in platform differences. Testing across many input combinations (fuzzing) is necessary because some discrepancies only appear under specific numeric or boundary conditions. Finding these systematically illuminates exactly which language features or data patterns cause porting problems, guiding developers on where workarounds are needed.

The core being retrieved are candidate paths through a knowledge graph that connect question terms to answers. The principle is that shortest paths are most trustworthy—if facts are connected by shorter chains, there are fewer steps where errors could accumulate—but only if paths are also semantically relevant to the question. The method works by finding multiple plausible paths of bounded length, scoring each based on whether the facts along it semantically match the question (using learned weights), then letting the language model reason over the best candidates. By encoding this reasoning in an iterative dialogue loop where the model can ask for different candidate sets, the system adapts retrieval when uncertain. This combination makes retrieval both efficient (fewer facts needed) and interpretable (users see which path was used to answer).

The core question is whether large language models can govern their own behavior through internal mechanisms. The principle being examined is that self-governance requires three things: monitoring your own actions, correcting behavior when it goes wrong, and actually caring about the values you're supposed to follow. The analysis shows models can do the first two to some extent—they can detect when outputs violate stated rules and adjust. However, they cannot do the third: they have no independent source of values to hold themselves accountable to beyond training and prompts. Without that grounding, self-regulation is shallow, more like following rules than genuinely believing in principles. This limitation means governance must remain external rather than purely internal.

The core challenge is matching stickers to user queries even when seeing new unseen stickers or expressing new communicative intents. The principle is that intent—the underlying communicative purpose—is abstract and shared across modality boundaries, while surface details (what stickers look like, what words are used) vary widely. By learning to represent both queries and stickers through their shared communicative intent rather than literal matching, the system generalizes to novel cases. This works because human intent is more stable than visual or textual surfaces—two very different stickers might express the same feeling. Cross-modal alignment (learning how intent translates between text and image) is the key: it teaches the system the abstraction that transcends specific training examples.

The core problem is aligning large models to multiple different human values that often conflict with each other. The principle is that values are consistent when satisfying one value doesn't require violating another on the same preference example—this internal coherence lets data from different value datasets be combined safely. The method works by filtering out preference examples where values conflict (high inconsistency) before training, ensuring the model learns smooth, non-contradictory patterns. When multiple smooth models trained on value-consistent data are combined, they can be merged without the performance drops that occur when mixing value-conflicting training signals. This filtering discipline lets a single model handle many values without expensive separate training for each combination.

The core being predicted is whether a link will appear in a dynamic network at a future time. The principle combining temporal-frequency analysis is that network changes happen at multiple timescales simultaneously: some patterns repeat quickly (hours), others unfold over days or weeks, and others are one-time events. By decomposing the temporal signal into multiple frequency bands simultaneously using wavelets, the system captures patterns at each scale independently. These multi-scale patterns are then fused using a model that understands both local wavelet details and global temporal trends. This multi-resolution approach works because the actual dynamics generating links operate at different speeds, and models must recognize patterns at every speed to predict accurately.

The core being measured is how different user behaviors on social platforms correlate with different information diets and ideologies. The principle is that behavior type (lurking, interacting, creating) mechanically determines what content you see—creators set the agenda by choosing what to post, interactors filter that feed through their choices, and lurkers passively receive what flows to them. Since each group controls different parts of the system, they end up exposed to different prevalence of controversial content. By using high-resolution activity logs instead of surveys, this study captures actual behavior patterns that users may not even realize they have. The finding that behavioral type predicts ideology suggests platform structures inadvertently create echo chambers organized by participation style, not just explicit choices.

The core being analyzed is community-driven content blocking as a moderation mechanism and its actual effects. The principle underlying this study is that visibility on social networks depends on reachability through connections, so blocking breaks links that prevent followers of the blocker from seeing blocked content. However, blocking only changes visibility in limited networks—it does not reduce the overall activity or popularity of blocked accounts. By measuring this transparency (mapping who blocks whom at scale and tracing consequences), the research shows that community blocking is not about suppressing disruptive users but about curating what individuals see. This finding reframes blocking as a personalization tool rather than a censorship mechanism, with implications for how decentralized moderation systems should be designed to stay resistant to coordinated control.
